newsitem.title: USA: Amoco says Inam could cost $2.5 billion.
newsitem.headline: Amoco says Inam could cost $2.5 billion.

text.p: Amoco Corp said on Friday that the development costs for the Inam field, some 120 miles south of the Azerbaijani capital of Baku, could be up to $2.5 billion if the field proves to be a success.

Luke Keller, vice president of Amoco's Caspian Sea operations, said in a conference call the company has yet to sign a production sharing agreement with the Azerbaijan, but had agreed to cooperate with the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan Republic in several projects in the upstream and the downstream sectors. One of these is to develop the Inam prospect in the South Caspian Sea.
Keller said that some 2-D seismic data had been shot over the area, but that it was too early to make any prediction of reserves.
He said that the field was around 100 meters deep in the shallow part and 200 meters in the deeper.
"We will start very soon to discuss the terms of a production sharing agreement," Keller said.
He added that Amoco would probably have to use a semisubmersible rather than a jackup rig to do any drilling.
Amoco does not plan to get involved in any refining in Azerbaijan, but will look at marketing and gasoline stations, although any stations would not bear the Amoco brand name, Keller said.

Asked whether he thought that the dispute over the status of the Caspian Sea created problems for foreign investors, Keller said: "The dispute over the area does cause us concern. We are confident that agreement will be reached among the littoral states."

The dispute stems from whether the landlocked Caspian is viewed as a lake or a sea and the five countries which border the Caspian are at loggerheads over how to split up the oil and natural gas deposits.
Russia and Iran say that it is a lake and so should be developed jointly by all sides, but Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan say that it is a sea and should be split into separate territories.
Keller said that he viewed the position "that a sectoral division to promote rapid development is in the best interests of the littoral states."
